{"id":"post_1790376615849_9ux3t0","type":"post","status":"published","title":"Unmasking Verho: A Conversation with Sebastian Solczak","subtitle":"SaikingS walks us along the path he carved, detailing what went into development of his most ambitious work yet!","slug":"unmasking-verho-a-conversation-with","slugCommitted":true,"date":"2026-07-26","tag":"","categories":[],"authors":["Andy"],"authorName":"Andy","authorInitial":"A","coverImage":"/blog/images/unmasking-verho-a-c-muimiu3j-hpab3.webp","navPrevTitle":"","navPrevSlug":"","navNextTitle":"","navNextSlug":"","overrideReadTime":"","customDesc":"","markdown":"![Image](/blog/images/unmasking-verho-a-c-muimiu3j-hpab3.webp) **First off, congrats on launching! I love your game so much. I can’t imagine how much effort it took. It’s officially been out for six months now, how does it feel?** > I feel really good! Before release, we had written out what theoretical Worst, Mid and Best scenarios post-launch could be. So far we are in the middle of Mid and Best so I’m really happy about that! It’s also amazing seeing people playing the game and giving their thoughts and feedback. **Kasur Games, the studio listed as Verho’s developer, has released more than just your game. How did your project get picked by them and grow into a team of people?** > I think of myself as the leader of the Verho team within [Kasur Games](https://kasur.games/). The studio founder and CEO, Tomasz Rusak, actually reached out about funding after the first year of development. That’s how Verho officially became a Kasur Games project. When it comes to my team, I did start off as a solo dev. Soon after work began, I invited [Valentino Cervini](https://valentinocervini.com/) onto the project to do musical composition. We’re good friends and have done lots of other projects together - most of which can be found on [my Itch.io account](https://saikings.itch.io/). Not long after that, I met Angelo “Grave” Petrilli on the King’s Field subreddit. We talked and he offered to handle sound design, thus joining the team! Close to the end of development, my friend Łukasz “Kaku” Fetliński joined. He helped with modeling some weapons and environmental assets so I could focus on polishing the final product. ![Image](/blog/images/unmasking-verho-a-c-muiolo0h-vr8t2.webp) **Is King’s Field-like an okay term for describing your game? How do you feel about games adopting that sort of a description?** > I’ve been calling this style of game King’s Field-like before I heard other people calling them that, so I like it! I think it’s a cool term even though these days a lot of people have switched to calling them Field-likes. Overall, it’s difficult to perfectly describe this genre of game, similar to Rogue-likes and Souls-likes. Everyone has a different definition of what these games truly are so it will probably stay this way. Who knows, maybe in a few years someone will come up with a more exact definition for King’s Field-likes and we’ll start saying that. **I bought my copy in a Steam bundle that included [Monomyth](https://store.steampowered.com/app/908360/Monomyth/). Now I see you can grab a copy along with [Fly Knight](https://store.steampowered.com/app/3108510/FlyKnight/) and several others! Is there a secret King’s Field Kabal? Or is this just an amazing time to be a fan?** > Most of that’s from devs I befriended while making Verho. We’re in an era of King’s Field-likes and will probably see more in the next 2-3 years. The question is how long people will be interested in them - I hope for a long time because I’ve always loved playing them! ![Image](/blog/images/unmasking-verho-a-c-muiomgjf-gnvtp.webp) **I was getting shades of the Shadow Temple from OoT in one of your game’s areas. As well as navigating the sands of Gerudo Valley! Would you mind revealing some of your undying inspirations?** > Fromsoft and Zelda were some of the biggest for sure. Another strong one is the Gothic series, especially the first 2 games. Lunacid by Akuma Kira felt huge, as did the King’s Field games themselves! I’ve played all of them including both Shadow Towers and Eternal Ring. I want to grasp the essence of those games so I can make things fans of them will enjoy. **Yariv (the setting of Verho) is a place with so much history. Entire generations have passed and shaped its structure. Everything about it felt so three dimensional and alive! Truly amazing work - have you always been a world builder?** > I just like making stories and universes. I have three to four big ones that I’ve written but never used. Maybe one day!The first thing I conceptualized about the Verho universe was the Curse of Faces [a curse that forces residents of Yariv always hide their face, lest they catch a glance of someone else’s face and die instantly.] Then I just kept building on the gaps and plot holes. There’s actually even more lore to the world than what’s shown in-game Some of it you can see in [“Verho - Curse of Faces - Behind The Mask”](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=74_Jy6dkHP4&list=PLITLonvIz3JUzMz-simuVeBO8c376KtsM&index=5), a lore series on YouTube we made with [CobraTekku Games](https://www.cobratekku.games/), our publisher. Some will be shown in expansion and future games. I have big plans for that world, but time will tell how I will be able to show it to everyone. ![Image](/blog/images/unmasking-verho-a-c-muionu92-wfsd8.webp) **Every location is so unique, undoubtedly hand crafted with love. I imagine most fans could see a screenshot of a random wall or corner of a structure and be able to pinpoint exactly where on the map that is. I’m dumbfounded - how did you pull this off?** > That’s funny! But a lot of Verho’s uniqueness is the product of me being kind of a bad 3D artist. I had never done modelling before so I just started making assets. I learned Blender for Verho. The more I did it, the better I became! A lot of cool things were actually the effect of me struggling to make something else. I’d need to pivot and would sometimes just let my imagination go wild!When it comes to the process, usually I draw a map of the area first, then start modeling. A negative side effect of that is that many of my maps turn out flat, something I’m kind of regretting and wish to fix on future projects. **There are a staggering amount of weapons and runes. Player customization is extensive, just about every play style seems viable and enemies just keep getting harder and harder. What was balancing all this like?** :::gallery /blog/images/unmasking-verho-a-c-muiop2aq-83wmv.webp /blog/images/unmasking-verho-a-c-muiop698-mgwz6.webp ::: :::caption Concept vs Final::: **The Omens were an enemy who stuck with me - the flying skeletons who teleport around the player and attack with moves that require 360-degrees of awareness. How you ended up on this design? They’re really satisfying to fight!** > It started with their concept art. When modelling, I decided to switch their skull heads for masks and made abilities based around each one. Foggy Borrows is also a pretty empty area so I was able to have enemies that can teleport and go through long distances. **I felt a little overpowered late game, using a three-hit combo that swung for 1500 per ‘turn’. Have you crushing builds from people in your community?** > Yeah, I’ve seen a lot of busted builds. I think it’s part of the fun , being a little overpowered in the late game! Especially if you explore a lot, do all the game’s content. It’s a part of the Field-like identity. ![Gallery image](/blog/images/unmasking-verho-a-c-muiw5fap-8jnbx.webp) **I imagine releasing Verho and living to tell the tale feels like sitting on top of a mountain, your perspective is more all-seeing than anyone could imagine. With your newly earned insight on life, do you wish to continue making games? Any plans for your future?** > I wouldn’t say I’m sitting at the top of a mountain. If so, then I can see MUCH bigger mountains around me! Kira having made Lunacid, Deep Denizens working on Hark the Ghoul, Freshly Baked Games making Queens Domain. So many others! I aspire to keep making better games until I’m on their level.For the soon-to-be projects, it’s not a secret that I’m working on Verho DLC. I hope to release that later this year! I’m also releasing Bonehold in July, that is my side project [being co-developed with Bloodcorvus, a dev who worked on the game Blood West]. After the Verho DLC, I would love to make the next Verho game - if it will be possible! Once again, I owe a huge THANK YOU to SaikingS for indulging my curiosity with this interview! I can’t say enough good about the game he put together - go **[buy it and play it on Steam](https://store.steampowered.com/app/3017330/Verho__Curse_of_Faces/)** right now, if you haven’t already!","proseHtml":"

First off, congrats on launching! I love your game so much. I can’t imagine how much effort it took. It’s officially been out for six months now, how does it feel?

I feel really good! Before release, we had written out what theoretical Worst, Mid and Best scenarios post-launch could be. So far we are in the middle of Mid and Best so I’m really happy about that! It’s also amazing seeing people playing the game and giving their thoughts and feedback.

Kasur Games, the studio listed as Verho’s developer, has released more than just your game. How did your project get picked by them and grow into a team of people?

I think of myself as the leader of the Verho team within Kasur Games. The studio founder and CEO, Tomasz Rusak, actually reached out about funding after the first year of development. That’s how Verho officially became a Kasur Games project.

When it comes to my team, I did start off as a solo dev. Soon after work began, I invited Valentino Cervini onto the project to do musical composition. We’re good friends and have done lots of other projects together - most of which can be found on my Itch.io account. Not long after that, I met Angelo “Grave” Petrilli on the King’s Field subreddit. We talked and he offered to handle sound design, thus joining the team! Close to the end of development, my friend Łukasz “Kaku” Fetliński joined. He helped with modeling some weapons and environmental assets so I could focus on polishing the final product.

Is King’s Field-like an okay term for describing your game? How do you feel about games adopting that sort of a description?

I’ve been calling this style of game King’s Field-like before I heard other people calling them that, so I like it! I think it’s a cool term even though these days a lot of people have switched to calling them Field-likes. Overall, it’s difficult to perfectly describe this genre of game, similar to Rogue-likes and Souls-likes. Everyone has a different definition of what these games truly are so it will probably stay this way. Who knows, maybe in a few years someone will come up with a more exact definition for King’s Field-likes and we’ll start saying that.

I bought my copy in a Steam bundle that included Monomyth. Now I see you can grab a copy along with Fly Knight and several others! Is there a secret King’s Field Kabal? Or is this just an amazing time to be a fan?

Most of that’s from devs I befriended while making Verho. We’re in an era of King’s Field-likes and will probably see more in the next 2-3 years. The question is how long people will be interested in them - I hope for a long time because I’ve always loved playing them!

I was getting shades of the Shadow Temple from OoT in one of your game’s areas. As well as navigating the sands of Gerudo Valley! Would you mind revealing some of your undying inspirations?

Fromsoft and Zelda were some of the biggest for sure. Another strong one is the Gothic series, especially the first 2 games. Lunacid by Akuma Kira felt huge, as did the King’s Field games themselves! I’ve played all of them including both Shadow Towers and Eternal Ring. I want to grasp the essence of those games so I can make things fans of them will enjoy.

Yariv (the setting of Verho) is a place with so much history. Entire generations have passed and shaped its structure. Everything about it felt so three dimensional and alive! Truly amazing work - have you always been a world builder?

I just like making stories and universes. I have three to four big ones that I’ve written but never used. Maybe one day!

The first thing I conceptualized about the Verho universe was the Curse of Faces [a curse that forces residents of Yariv always hide their face, lest they catch a glance of someone else’s face and die instantly.] Then I just kept building on the gaps and plot holes. There’s actually even more lore to the world than what’s shown in-game Some of it you can see in “Verho - Curse of Faces - Behind The Mask”, a lore series on YouTube we made with CobraTekku Games, our publisher. Some will be shown in expansion and future games. I have big plans for that world, but time will tell how I will be able to show it to everyone.

Every location is so unique, undoubtedly hand crafted with love. I imagine most fans could see a screenshot of a random wall or corner of a structure and be able to pinpoint exactly where on the map that is. I’m dumbfounded - how did you pull this off?

That’s funny! But a lot of Verho’s uniqueness is the product of me being kind of a bad 3D artist. I had never done modelling before so I just started making assets. I learned Blender for Verho. The more I did it, the better I became! A lot of cool things were actually the effect of me struggling to make something else. I’d need to pivot and would sometimes just let my imagination go wild!

When it comes to the process, usually I draw a map of the area first, then start modeling. A negative side effect of that is that many of my maps turn out flat, something I’m kind of regretting and wish to fix on future projects.

There are a staggering amount of weapons and runes. Player customization is extensive, just about every play style seems viable and enemies just keep getting harder and harder. What was balancing all this like?

Concept vs Final

The Omens were an enemy who stuck with me - the flying skeletons who teleport around the player and attack with moves that require 360-degrees of awareness. How you ended up on this design? They’re really satisfying to fight!

It started with their concept art. When modelling, I decided to switch their skull heads for masks and made abilities based around each one. Foggy Borrows is also a pretty empty area so I was able to have enemies that can teleport and go through long distances.

I felt a little overpowered late game, using a three-hit combo that swung for 1500 per ‘turn’. Have you crushing builds from people in your community?

Yeah, I’ve seen a lot of busted builds. I think it’s part of the fun , being a little overpowered in the late game! Especially if you explore a lot, do all the game’s content. It’s a part of the Field-like identity.

I imagine releasing Verho and living to tell the tale feels like sitting on top of a mountain, your perspective is more all-seeing than anyone could imagine. With your newly earned insight on life, do you wish to continue making games? Any plans for your future?

I wouldn’t say I’m sitting at the top of a mountain. If so, then I can see MUCH bigger mountains around me! Kira having made Lunacid, Deep Denizens working on Hark the Ghoul, Freshly Baked Games making Queens Domain. So many others! I aspire to keep making better games until I’m on their level.

For the soon-to-be projects, it’s not a secret that I’m working on Verho DLC. I hope to release that later this year! I’m also releasing Bonehold in July, that is my side project [being co-developed with Bloodcorvus, a dev who worked on the game Blood West]. After the Verho DLC, I would love to make the next Verho game - if it will be possible!

Once again, I owe a huge THANK YOU to SaikingS for indulging my curiosity with this interview! I can’t say enough good about the game he put together - go buy it and play it on Steam right now, if you haven’t already!

I bailed on Halloween plans tonight. On one hand, I'm bummed to have let people down, on the other I'm incredibly excited to have resecured more time for my self-imposed crunch.

I want to give a rundown of everything on my plate, game design wise —

Silent Hill — First-Person Mod

I really wish I would have gotten this one done by Halloween. I absolutely could have, as it's my first attempt add using AI to mod games. It's in a super playable state as is, my partner got all the way to Midwich Elementary without hassle.

Putting this game in first-person is probably pretty divisive to some, but I wanted to see what it was like and tbh I love it! Between the shift in camera perspective and the port's rendering at a higher resolution, you can really admire how much work the original developers put into every scene's detail. The combat gets easier when you're decent at aiming in first-person but honestly, who's playing this game for the combat? I think a 'no enemies' mod would arguably make this game even better for some people! The Alchemilla HL2 mod was that for me, as was the passive monster SOMA mod.

I don't want to change much of the core game, but I was thinking about making some 'vanilla plus' mods the player could toggle. My first ideas is to have the radio get loud when you're around key items because holy moly was it painful wandering around the town of Silent Hill looking for keys before getting to Midwich. I got a feeling playing through the game and making changes as I go is going to be the easiest way to uncover potential changes like this, but with all my other projects... yea, that ain't happening any time soon lol

Shouts to the SH decomp project PLUS the SH PC port projects for building a moddable base!

Far Cry 1 — Modernized QOL Upgrades

Here's where my attention has REALLY been going. I was researching which games allow for the greatest ease of modding and surprisingly Far Cry 1 was incredibly high on the list. Almost everything about the game is written in Lua, meaning almost all of the game logic is completely readable! Additionally, Crytek released many of their dll's via official modding tools back in the day, so aside from a few small files, almost nothing is black boxed.

I've honestly hated playing vanilla FC1. Even back in the day, running it on my family's computer, I could tell just how janky so many things about it are. So having a means of turning into pretty much whatever game I want is mesmerizing!

First thing I added was real iron sights to all the weapons. Several of the scoped weapons really didn't benefit from the scope, so I opened them up in Blender and touched each one up to rely on the real thing (not the AG36 in the image above. Next, I used the flip phone model to make a more diegetic way of seeing the mini-map and the game objectives. Then I added bandages and armor plates for players to have more control over how they monitor their health.

Controversial change - I made a S.T.A.L.K.E.R. style inventory system to manage these new pickups as well as weapons, but tbh I'm considering rolling that change back and focusing on making a more minimalist UI. Reason being, Far Cry is just straight up built to be an arcade shooter. Unless I wanted to SERIOUSLY overhaul the game (which I'm considering doing for a different mod) then I'd be changing the core more than I wish for.

This iteration really was just suppose to be a 'modernization' of the game and other than bugs and rebalances that I'm still working on, I think we're pretty much there.

Chernobyl Commando — Literally just make it playable & fun

Last minute last night, I tried this one out. It's an old Polish game made by Silden whom I believe are ex-City Interactive employees. They broke away, licensed the CI engine (Argon 5 to be specific) and made... welp, it is certainly a game-like product!

The Steam page for the game still exists if you're interested but it can't be purchased through anywhere but key sites. It's literally unplayable on modern Windows though I did get the game to boot on Linux via Proton but the main character fell through the ground indefinitely when the very first segment begins.

I managed to get it running by using a headless version of Ghidra to help translate the launcher into something the AI could work with. It told me about LOTS of fault that prevented it from launching, one of them being a bottleneck that would make the game refuse to launch until every single process on your computer acknowledge that it was going to load two temporary fonts into a global process. Idk if that's funny or typical but I think it's pretty goofy.

Now that the game is working it's... pretty horrible. Thought it's got a great art style, the architecture is super interesting (though I wouldn't say the level design is good...) and it's got a handful of guns that all feel and sound pretty good to control. I'm going to keep patching the hell out of it, see what it turns into.

Back when physical PC games were sold for five bucks at newsstands and grocery checkouts, studios like Silden — using what seems to be a fork of City Interactive’s engine — churned out budget shooters by the truckload. Most people look back at these games as bargain-bin trash. But to an OG first-person shooter fan, there is something endlessly fascinating about seeing what these low-budget oddities were trying to pull off.

Enter Chernobyl Commando.

It’s an objectively rough game, and for the longest time, modern hardware simply refused to touch it. Most people online assumed it was legacy OS incompatibilities, modern frame-rate issues, or missing service packs. The first time I ever got a pulse out of it was messing around on my Steam Deck. Believe it or not, Proton handled Chernobyl Commando on the very first try.

The catch? I loaded into the first level and immediately fell straight through the bottom of the map into the void. At that point, I figured the game was permanently unplayable unless you happened to own a budget PC from 2010.

Lately, though, I’ve been experimenting with vibe coding and using AI to build new fixing pipelines for abandoned retro games. I figured: why not see what AI could do for Chernobyl Commando?

Side note: Despite being abandonware, a Steam page for it still exists. I bought my copy on Kinguin for probably nickel years ago and is why I've had this game on my radar for so long. Was peaking around the community stuff and saw a stupid screenshot from someone with the Dusk logo as their profile pic. Curiously, I clicked the profile and sure enough, it actually was David who posted this. I don't know him personally, but I see his name associated with so much obscure shit online that he's practically an FPS cryptid.

Fixing the Unplayable

After a couple of hours tinkering with assistance from Gemini, we got it to load properly. I mentioned the infinite-falling bug and Gemini actually tracked down the root cause. It turned out to be an engine logic quirk documented in some Polish pseudo-code with its failure to run properly resulting in an endless freefall.

gun_dismount <target> – zmusza gracza do puszczenia broni statycznej i teleportuje gracza do targetu — powinien być blisko pozycji broni, 2-3 metry góra, albo podróż będzie długa.

Translation: "Forces the player to let go of the static weapon and teleports the player to the target — it should be close to the weapon's position, 2–3 meters max, otherwise it's going to be a loooong trip."

Once the game was finally running, actually playing it was a whole new nightmare:

  • Stuttering Movement: You couldn’t walk four feet without your forward input randomly getting swallowed. You had to constantly tap W just to cross a room.
  • Absurd Sprinting: Sprints moved at lightspeed—likely a physics tick-rate bug tied to framerate — only to slam you to an immediate dead stop.
  • Blinding Gunplay: The iron sights were atrocious. Weapon recoil produced so much visual noise that you couldn’t see what you were shooting at, and enemies barely flinched when hit.
  • Pacing Killers: Load screens took an agonizing 30+ seconds, and checkpoint saves would literally freeze the screen for half a second while flashing a massive "GAME SAVED" banner across the display.

I went to work smoothing out the rough edges. I rebuilt the sprint curve, implemented a proper leaning mechanic, smoothed out the gun recoil, added hit markers so shots felt tangible, and built an internal debug tool so I could manually reposition the weapon models for both hip-fire and ADS. I even eliminated the save stutter and cut load times down to nothing.

To my shock, once those core issues were patched, the game didn't fight back. I played through nearly half the campaign, only needing to prompt the AI for a few minor edge-case fixes along the way.

The Real Problem: Mechanics Can't Fix Game Design

Here's the irony of deep-modding bad games: once you make the mechanics feel smooth, you strip away the buffer that hides just how bad the core game really is.

Underneath the jank, Chernobyl Commando is a brain-dead, strictly linear arcade gallery. What makes it tragic is the world design. It drops you into these massive, visually intriguing environments that look like an open-world survival game. You look out at the horizon and imagine what it would be like to explore it.

Except you can’t.

There is zero reason to wander, and the game actively punishes curiosity. Step off the intended dirt track, and a kill-countdown instantly flashes on screen, threatening to fail your mission if you don’t sprint back to the main road immediately.

There are no real set pieces, either. The "high points" of the campaign consist entirely of:

  1. Walk up to an RPK, shoot a wave of guys. Hop on the back of a truck, shoot another wave of guys.
  2. Be told "Hurry, get over here!", shoot a corridor of guys on the way there, hit an invisible trigger, and watch the screen fade to black before dumping you into the next level.

Not all jank is good jank.

When I mod something like Far Cry to be mechanically tighter, or add a divisive First-Person mode to the PC port of Silent Hill, the payoff is immense. I'm left with a personalized, definitive version of a game I want to like more.

With Chernobyl Commando, tightening the screws just makes me realize that to make it fun, I'd need to scrap everything and build an entirely different game inside the shell.

I’ll still finish the campaign, and once the project is packaged up, I'll release the fixes so anyone morbidly curious can experience it without the launch-breaking bugs. But it won't get the victory lap of my other restoration projects.

Some games — like Alien Rage, which had wild bugs and brainless shooting but carried a bold, distinctive style — make the troubleshooting journey part of the charm. Chernobyl Commando is just a reminder of a bygone budget era: weird, broken, and probably best left in the newsstand bargain bin.

After a decade-plus of experimenting with blogging tools, I never found one I really liked. Cedar is my attempt at pulling the best parts of classic writers into a single, focused experience.

Cedar is an open-source, web-based static blog generator built to keep writing simple. Out of the box, it:

  • Gives you a focused writing studio for drafting and formatting posts.
  • Manages your posts, pages, and media in one place.
  • Organizes your static site files automatically so they are always ready to publish.
  • Makes deploying effortless—whether pushing straight to GitHub or exporting a .zip.

100% Local-First

Even though Cedar runs in your browser, everything you create stays 100% on your machine until you choose to move it elsewhere. You can work directly in your browser's local storage, save your project to a folder on your computer or a portable SSD, or publish straight to GitHub.

Whatever your workflow, Cedar handles the file structure behind the scenes—so you get all the speed and ownership of a static site without ever having to wrestle with files and folders.

Try Cedar at cedar.pub  •  View Source on GitHub
